topics.title: Pressure gradient force and Coriolis effect
lesson: Wind is air moving in response to forces. Two forces explain most large-scale wind: the pressure gradient force and the Coriolis effect.
The PGF pushes air from high toward low pressure, perpendicular to the isobars. The closer the isobars, the larger the gradient and the stronger the force. On a chart, tight isobars mean strong wind.

list: An apparent force caused by Earth's rotation. It deflects moving air to the RIGHT in the Northern Hemisphere and to the LEFT in the Southern Hemisphere.
It changes direction only, never speed.
It is zero at the equator and greatest at the poles. It grows with wind speed.
It is too small to matter for small, short-lived motions such as a sea breeze over a few hours.

lesson: Stand with your back to the wind. Low pressure is on your left. This works above the friction layer, where the wind is close to geostrophic.

lesson.note: Air does not blow straight from high to low. The Coriolis effect turns it until it flows around the pressure centres.

terms: Line joining points of equal pressure.
Rate of change of pressure with horizontal distance.
Apparent deflection of moving air due to Earth's rotation.

questions.q: In which direction does the pressure gradient force act?
c: From high to low pressure, perpendicular to isobars
From low to high pressure, perpendicular to the isobars
Parallel to the isobars with high pressure on the right
Toward the equator along the nearest line of latitude
questions.e: The PGF points from high to low pressure at right angles to the isobars.

questions.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, the Coriolis effect deflects moving air:
questions.e: Northern Hemisphere deflection is to the right of the direction of motion.

questions.q: What is the Coriolis effect at the equator?
questions.e: It is proportional to sin(latitude), which is zero at the equator.

questions.q: Buys Ballot's law in the Northern Hemisphere: with your back to the wind, where is low pressure?
questions.e: In the Northern Hemisphere low pressure is on the left when your back is to the wind.

questions.q: What does close isobar spacing on a surface chart indicate?
questions.e: Closely spaced isobars mean a steep pressure gradient, hence a strong wind.

questions.q: In the Southern Hemisphere the Coriolis effect deflects moving air:
c: To the left of its direction of motion
To the right of its direction of motion
questions.e: The Southern Hemisphere deflection is opposite to the Northern Hemisphere: to the left.

questions.q: Which statement about the Coriolis effect is correct?
c: It changes the direction of motion but not the speed
It speeds up air that flows poleward and slows air flowing toward the equator
It is strongest at the equator and falls to zero at the poles
It acts only on air above the boundary layer, not near the ground
questions.e: Coriolis acts at right angles to the motion, so it cannot change speed.

questions.q: Isobars 4 hPa apart are 100 km apart in one area and 200 km apart in another. Where is the pressure gradient force larger?
c: Where they are 100 km apart, by a factor of two
Where they are 200 km apart, by a factor of two
They are the same in both areas
Neither, because spacing does not affect the force
questions.e: The gradient is pressure change per distance: 4/100 is twice 4/200.

questions.q: Why is geostrophic balance not valid near the equator?
c: The Coriolis effect goes to zero
questions.e: Coriolis is proportional to the sine of latitude and vanishes at 0 degrees.

questions.q: Stand with your back to the wind in the Northern Hemisphere and low pressure is on your left. Which rule is this?
questions.e: Buys Ballot's law locates pressure systems from the wind direction.

questions.q: Which factor does the Coriolis force depend on?
questions.e: Coriolis force increases with wind speed and with the sine of latitude.

sources: Penn State METEO 3, Introductory Meteorology: forces on wind: PGF direction, Coriolis to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, grows with speed and latitude, geostrophic wind parallel to isobars, Buys Ballot's law
AMS Glossary, Coriolis parameter: f = 2 Omega sin(latitude); zero at the equator follows from the formula (the page does not state it)
unverified: Source is a university course text, not a Canadian government publication.

Coriolis zero at the equator is derived from the AMS formula. Coriolis changing direction but not speed, and 'too small for sea breezes': standard physics, not stated on any page read. Single source for the formula (AMS); consistent with the Penn State page already used.

topics.title: Geostrophic, gradient and thermal wind
lesson: Above the friction layer, for straight isobars, the pressure gradient force balances the Coriolis force. The wind then blows parallel to the isobars with low pressure on the left (Northern Hemisphere). Wind speed is proportional to the pressure gradient.

Real isobars curve. Around a low, the net force toward the centre must supply the centripetal force, so the gradient wind is slower than the geostrophic wind for the same pressure gradient (subgeostrophic). Around a high, it is faster (supergeostrophic).
The thermal wind is not a real wind. It is the vector difference between the geostrophic winds at two levels. It blows parallel to the thickness lines with cold air on the left (Northern Hemisphere).

list: A strong horizontal temperature gradient means wind increases rapidly with height. This is why jet streams sit above frontal zones.
Wind turning counterclockwise with height (backing) means cold air advection.
Wind turning clockwise with height (veering) means warm air advection.

lesson.note: Quick check: if the wind veers (turns clockwise) with height in a sounding, warm air is arriving. If it backs, cold air is arriving.

terms: Wind resulting from balance between PGF and Coriolis force, parallel to straight isobars.
Wind that also accounts for curvature of the flow.
Vector difference of geostrophic wind between two levels, parallel to thickness lines.
Counterclockwise / clockwise turning of wind direction.

questions.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, the geostrophic wind blows:
c: Parallel to isobars with low pressure on the left
Parallel to isobars with low pressure on the right
questions.e: PGF and Coriolis balance, so flow runs along the isobars with low pressure to the left.

questions.q: Around a low-pressure centre, how does the gradient wind compare with the geostrophic wind for the same pressure gradient?
questions.e: Around a low the pressure gradient force must also supply the centripetal force, so the wind is slower than geostrophic.

questions.q: In the Northern Hemisphere the thermal wind blows parallel to thickness lines with:
questions.e: The thermal wind keeps the cold air to the left, just as the geostrophic wind keeps low pressure to the left.

questions.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, winds that back (turn counterclockwise) with height indicate:
questions.e: Backing with height signals cold advection; veering with height signals warm advection (Albany ATM 317 thermal wind notes).

questions.q: Why are jet streams found above frontal zones?
c: A strong horizontal temperature gradient makes wind increase rapidly with height
Surface friction is weakest along frontal boundaries, so winds aloft strengthen
Condensation in frontal cloud releases heat that directly accelerates the upper wind
The Coriolis force is strongest where fronts lie, which speeds up the flow aloft
questions.e: Thermal wind balance means a large horizontal temperature contrast produces a large increase in wind with height.

questions.q: Above the friction layer, the wind blows:
c: Straight from high to low pressure
Opposite to the pressure gradient force
questions.e: Above the friction layer the wind is close to geostrophic and follows the isobars.

questions.q: Around a high-pressure centre the gradient wind compared with the geostrophic wind (same gradient) is:
c: Equal to the geostrophic wind in every case
Zero, because the centrifugal force cancels the wind
questions.e: Around highs the force balance allows a stronger wind for the same pressure gradient.

questions.q: The thermal wind blows parallel to which lines?
c: Surface isobars, because the thermal wind is just the surface wind
Frontal boundaries on the surface chart and nothing else
Jet axis wind maxima at the 250 hPa level only
questions.e: Thermal wind follows the thickness lines, with cold air on the left in the Northern Hemisphere.

questions.q: Winds that veer (turn clockwise) with height in the Northern Hemisphere indicate:
questions.e: Veering with height is the signature of warm advection in the Northern Hemisphere.

questions.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, cold air lies to the north and warm air to the south. How does a westerly wind change with height?
c: It reverses to easterly at once
questions.e: A north-south temperature gradient gives westerly thermal wind, so westerlies strengthen aloft.

questions.q: Which of these winds is best approximated by balance between the pressure gradient force and the Coriolis force?
questions.e: Local circulations are driven by heating or terrain, while the geostrophic wind is a large-scale balance.

sources: University at Albany ATM 317, Thermal Wind notes: thermal wind is the vector difference of geostrophic winds, parallel to thickness lines with cold air on the left; backing = cold advection, veering = warm advection
LibreTexts, Jet streams: thermal wind as vertical shear of the geostrophic wind caused by a horizontal temperature gradient
Penn State METEO 3: geostrophic wind parallel to isobars
AMS Glossary, Gradient wind: cyclonic curvature is subgeostrophic, anticyclonic is supergeostrophic
University at Albany ATM 316, Balanced flow: same statements for the same pressure gradient (two sources agree)
unverified: Wind speed proportional to pressure gradient and geostrophic balance above the friction layer: partly confirmed (geostrophic definition, 'often close at high altitudes').
Wind speed proportional to pressure gradient is true for geostrophic flow only. Gradient wind curvature effects are now confirmed by two sources (AMS, Albany).

topics.title: Friction and boundary layer winds
lesson: The atmospheric boundary layer is the lowest part of the troposphere, in direct contact with the surface, where friction and turbulence matter. It has no fixed depth: from tens of metres under strongly stable conditions to several kilometres in strongly convective conditions (AMS Glossary). Friction slows the wind. A slower wind feels a weaker Coriolis effect, so the pressure gradient force wins and the wind turns toward lower pressure.

list: Surface wind blows across the isobars toward low pressure: about 30 degrees on average over land (Penn State), less over water, and 45 degrees or more over mountainous terrain (Penn State). Albany gives about 20 to 40 degrees over land and 10 to 20 degrees over water.
Friction slows the wind, so surface wind is weaker than the geostrophic wind. The usual fractions (about one-third to one-half over land, two-thirds over water) were not confirmed and were removed.
Surface winds therefore back (turn counterclockwise) relative to the wind above. Wind veers with height through the friction layer.

lesson: Around a surface low, the air spirals inward (converges) and rises, which supports cloud and precipitation. Around a surface high it spirals outward (diverges) and air sinks from above, which suppresses cloud.

list: Daytime: surface heating drives vigorous turbulence in a mixed layer that deepens over the day (AMS Glossary). Stronger winds aloft are brought down, so gusts peak in the afternoon (standard teaching).

Night: near sunset turbulence weakens and the bottom of the layer becomes a stable boundary layer over the cooled surface (AMS Glossary). Surface wind drops while winds just above can strengthen (see low-level jets).

lesson.note: Rougher terrain (forest, cities) gives more friction, less surface wind, and greater turning than open water.

terms: Lowest part of the atmosphere directly influenced by surface friction, about 1 to 2 km deep.
Net horizontal inflow of air toward a point.
Net horizontal outflow of air from a point.
Brief increase in wind speed above the mean.

questions.q: How does the surface wind compare with the geostrophic wind above the friction layer?
c: Slower and turned toward lower pressure
Faster and parallel to the isobars
Slower and turned toward higher pressure
questions.e: Friction slows the wind, weakens Coriolis, and lets the pressure gradient force turn the flow toward low pressure.

questions.q: How does surface air flow around a Northern Hemisphere low?
questions.e: Northern Hemisphere lows have counterclockwise circulation with inflow (convergence) at the surface.

questions.q: Over which surface is the turning angle between surface wind and isobars generally largest?
questions.e: Penn State: about 30 degrees on average over land, less over water, 45 degrees or more in mountains. Rougher surfaces turn the wind more.

questions.q: Why do surface gusts often peak in the afternoon?
c: Daytime heating mixes faster upper winds down to the surface
Pressure gradients over land are strongest at noon each day
Friction between wind and ground is lowest in the afternoon hours
The Coriolis effect reaches its daily maximum in the early afternoon
questions.e: Convective mixing during the day transports momentum from aloft downward.

questions.q: What does the air do over a surface high-pressure centre?
c: Diverges at the surface while air sinks from above
Converges at the surface while air rises through the column
Stays nearly stationary with no vertical motion above it
Spirals counterclockwise and inward toward the central pressure
questions.e: Surface divergence in a high is replaced by sinking air, which suppresses cloud.

questions.q: Compared with open water, friction effects over forested terrain are:
c: Greater, giving slower surface winds turned more across the isobars
Smaller, giving faster surface winds that blow nearly parallel to the isobars
Identical, because roughness does not change speed or direction at all
Reversed, so the surface wind blows toward higher pressure over forest
questions.e: Rougher surfaces slow the wind more and increase its turning toward low pressure.

questions.q: Which statement about the depth of the atmospheric boundary layer is correct?
c: It varies from tens of metres when stable to several km when convective
It is a fixed layer 1 to 2 km deep everywhere and at all times
It is always about 100 m deep because friction stops at that height
It always reaches the tropopause at every latitude and season
questions.e: AMS Glossary: the top of the layer, the inversion height, changes with time and place, from tens of metres in strongly stable conditions to several km in convective ones.

questions.q: On a clear night with a strong surface inversion, surface winds usually:
c: Decrease while winds a few hundred metres up may increase
Increase because of strong mixing from the winds aloft all night
Reverse direction completely as the inversion forms after sunset
Match the geostrophic wind exactly because friction vanishes at night
questions.e: The inversion decouples the surface layer so winds near the ground drop.

questions.q: Surface convergence beneath a low leads to:
c: Sinking air that gives clear skies and no precipitation
No vertical motion at all, only horizontal inflow
A strong subsidence inversion aloft over the low
questions.e: Air that flows inward has nowhere to go but up.

questions.q: A pilot descends toward the surface in the Northern Hemisphere through the friction layer. How does the wind direction usually change?
c: It backs (turns counterclockwise) as height decreases
It veers (turns clockwise) as height decreases toward the ground
It stays exactly the same through the whole friction layer
It reverses by 180 degrees close to the ground
questions.e: Friction turns the wind toward low pressure, which means backing as you approach the ground.

questions.q: What most reduces surface wind speed compared with the geostrophic wind?
questions.e: Friction slows the near-surface air and breaks the geostrophic balance.

sources: Penn State METEO 3: friction slows the wind; crossing angle about 30 degrees over land, less over water, 45 degrees or more in mountains
AMS Glossary, Atmospheric boundary layer: no fixed depth, tens of metres to several km; mixed layer deepens by day; stable layer at night
University at Albany, SHW Ch. 7: friction turns the wind 20 to 40 degrees over land and 10 to 20 degrees over water (agrees with Penn State's 30 degree average)
unverified: Speed fractions of surface to geostrophic wind were removed (no source).
Afternoon gust peak, and surface convergence under lows and divergence under highs: standard teaching, not confirmed on the pages read (Albany says friction weakens surface highs and lows).

topics.title: General circulation (Hadley, Ferrel, Polar cells)
lesson: The sun heats the tropics more than the poles. The atmosphere moves heat poleward in a pattern called the general circulation. In each hemisphere it is simplified into three cells.

list: Hadley cell (0 to 30 degrees): air rises at the ITCZ near the equator, flows poleward aloft, sinks at about 30 degrees. Surface flow returns toward the equator as the trade winds.
Ferrel cell (30 to 60 degrees): an indirect, eddy-driven cell. Surface flow is poleward and turned into westerlies.
Polar cell (60 to 90 degrees): cold air sinks at the pole and flows equatorward as polar easterlies.
ITCZ (near the equator): low pressure, rising air, heavy rain, light winds (doldrums).
Subtropical highs (about 30 degrees): sinking air, clear skies, deserts. The Azores/Bermuda High affects Atlantic weather.
Polar front (about 60 degrees): boundary between polar and mid-latitude air. Mid-latitude cyclones form along it.
Trade winds: from the northeast in the Northern Hemisphere and southeast in the Southern.
Prevailing westerlies in mid-latitudes. Nova Scotia sits in this belt, so weather mostly arrives from the west.

lesson.note: The real circulation is not three tidy cells. Waves and eddies carry much of the heat poleward at mid-latitudes. The cells are a teaching model.

terms: Intertropical Convergence Zone: band of rising air and heavy convection near the equator.
Steady easterly surface winds between the equator and about 30 degrees.
Prevailing winds from the west in mid-latitudes.
Boundary between polar and mid-latitude air masses, near 60 degrees.

questions.q: Which three cells make up the simplified general circulation in each hemisphere?
questions.e: The three-cell model has Hadley (tropical), Ferrel (mid-latitude) and Polar cells.

questions.q: The trade winds in the Northern Hemisphere blow from the:
questions.e: Trade winds are easterlies; in the Northern Hemisphere they come from the northeast.

questions.q: What conditions characterize the subtropical highs near 30 degrees latitude?
c: Sinking air, clear skies and dry conditions
Rising air, deep cloud and heavy tropical rainfall
Strong fronts, frequent cyclones and persistent storm tracks
Persistent fog, drizzle and light onshore winds all year
questions.e: The Hadley cell descends near 30 degrees, producing dry, stable conditions and many of the world's deserts.

questions.q: What is the prevailing wind direction over Nova Scotia?
questions.e: Nova Scotia lies in the mid-latitude westerlies.

questions.q: Which cell is considered 'indirect' and driven mainly by eddies?
questions.e: The Ferrel cell is driven by mid-latitude eddies rather than direct thermal forcing.

questions.q: Which describes the ITCZ?
c: Rising air, deep convection, heavy rain and light winds
Sinking air, clear dry weather and strong steady trade winds
Persistent low stratus and fog with light drizzle all year
Polar easterlies meeting the westerlies with frequent fronts
questions.e: The ITCZ is the equatorial zone of convergence and deep convection.

questions.q: The polar easterlies blow from the:
c: West toward the mid-latitudes, steered by the jet stream aloft
South toward the pole, then curving back into the westerlies
North toward the equator, becoming the northeast trade winds
questions.e: Polar easterlies flow from the east at high latitudes.

questions.q: Why do many deserts lie near 30 degrees latitude?
c: Dry air sinks in the descending branch of the Hadley cell
Moist air rises there from the ITCZ and drops its rain nearby
Polar-front storms cross the area every few days in the winter
Cold ocean currents alone cool the coast and prevent any rainfall
questions.e: Sinking air warms and dries, suppressing cloud and rain.

questions.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, Coriolis turns the equatorward surface flow of the Hadley cell into:
questions.e: Equatorward flow is turned to the right and becomes the northeast trades.

questions.q: Where is the polar front typically located?
questions.e: The polar front separates polar and mid-latitude air near 60 degrees.

questions.q: Which of these cells is NOT thermally direct?
questions.e: Hadley and Polar cells are direct; the Ferrel cell is indirect and eddy-driven.

sources: NWS Atmospheric Circulations training notes: three-cell model with highs near 30 and 90 degrees and lows near 0 and 60; ITCZ where NE and SE trades converge; subtropical highs with sinking air and deserts; northeast trades; westerlies; polar easterlies; polar front near 60 degrees as a zone where storms form

Colorado State, Global circulation notes: Ferrel cell indirect and eddy-driven (rises near 60, sinks near 30), ITCZ as rising branch of the Hadley cell, doldrums near the equator, trade winds either side
unverified: Exact latitude edges of each cell (0 to 30, 30 to 60, 60 to 90) follow from the pressure belts but are not stated as such.
Ferrel cell and doldrums now sourced to Colorado State notes (single new source; consistent with the NWS notes already used). The Colorado State page did not describe the polar cell.

topics.title: Jet streams
lesson: Jet streams are narrow, fast ribbons of wind near the tropopause. FAA AC 00-6A classifies a jet stream as winds of 50 kt or more and calls that figure arbitrary. The AMS Glossary also marks a jet on upper-level charts where the wind is reliably at least 50 kt. Belgium's national weather service (RMI) gives a minimum of 30 m/s (108 km/h, about 58 kt), the figure usually credited to the WMO, but the WMO document itself was not read. A US Navy text credits the WMO with dimensions of thousands of km long, hundreds of km wide and a few km deep. FAA gives lengths of 1,000 to 3,000 miles and widths of roughly 100 to 400 miles, in a narrow, shallow stream.

list: Polar front jet: near 50 to 60 degrees latitude and about 10 km up (roughly 250 to 300 hPa). Follows the polar front and shifts north and south. It moves farther south in winter.
Subtropical jet: near 30 degrees latitude and about 13 km up, above the tropical high.
Jets are strongest in winter because the equator-to-pole temperature contrast is greatest. Typical speeds are well above 100 kt in a core (LibreTexts).

lesson: Thermal wind balance: a strong horizontal temperature gradient in the lower atmosphere means wind increases with height until the temperature gradient reverses near the tropopause. The wind then peaks there.

Air accelerates into the jet core (entrance) and decelerates out of it (exit). In the Northern Hemisphere, upper-level divergence and rising air are favoured in the right entrance and left exit regions; convergence and sinking air are in the left entrance and right exit regions (NWS Louisville, MetEd, EUMeTrain, University at Albany all agree). Surface cyclones are favoured beneath the right entrance and left exit. In a jet streak at the base of a trough, the strongest divergence is in the left exit region on the northeast side of the trough, where strong surface cyclones develop (Albany).

Flying east with a jet saves time and fuel. Clear-air turbulence (CAT) is common near jet cores. FAA names the cold (polar) side in an upper trough as a preferred location, because wind speed falls off faster on that side and shear is greater.

lesson.note: Jet streams are found in the 250 hPa and 300 hPa charts. Look for tightly packed isotachs (lines of equal wind speed).

terms: Axis of maximum wind speed in a jet stream.
Clear-air turbulence: turbulence in cloudless air, often near jets, preferred on the polar side in an upper trough (FAA).

questions.q: What minimum wind speed does FAA AC 00-6A use to classify a jet stream?
questions.e: FAA AC 00-6A: 50 knots or greater, which the text calls arbitrary. Belgium's RMI gives 30 m/s (about 58 kt) as its minimum; the WMO document itself was not read.

questions.q: What is the main cause of jet streams?
c: A strong horizontal temperature gradient (thermal wind)
Surface friction acting on the flow along ocean coastlines
Mountain ranges forcing the air to speed up as it climbs
Warm ocean currents heating the air directly beneath the jet
questions.e: Strong temperature contrast produces strong vertical wind shear, which is largest near the tropopause.

questions.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, where is upper-level divergence favoured around a straight jet?
questions.e: Right entrance and left exit regions are the divergent quadrants and promote surface cyclogenesis below.

questions.q: Why are jet streams strongest in winter?
c: The equator-to-pole temperature contrast is greatest
The sun is closer to the Earth during Northern winter
Surface friction over snow-covered land is much lower
More cloud forms in winter and releases extra latent heat
questions.e: A larger temperature gradient gives stronger thermal wind and faster jets.

questions.q: Which chart is best for finding the polar front jet?
questions.e: The polar front jet sits near 250 to 300 hPa, close to the tropopause.

questions.q: At about which pressure level is the polar front jet usually strongest?
questions.e: The polar front jet is near the tropopause, around 250 to 300 hPa (about 10 km).

questions.q: A jet core of 120 kt is about how many metres per second?
questions.e: 1 kt is 0.514 m/s, so 120 kt is about 62 m/s.

questions.q: Where is clear-air turbulence most likely?
c: Near jet cores and strong shear zones
In the middle of a stable high, where winds are light
Near the surface in dense fog and calm conditions
Above 30 km in the stratosphere, well above the jet
questions.e: CAT is associated with strong vertical and horizontal wind shear near jets.

questions.q: Why does an eastbound flight from Halifax to London benefit from the jet stream?
c: The jet flows from west to east, giving a tailwind
The jet flows from east to west, giving a tailwind
The jet flows north to south, giving a crosswind only
The jet exists only at the equator
questions.e: Mid-latitude jets blow from the west, so eastbound flights get a tailwind.

questions.q: How does the Northern Hemisphere jet stream usually change from winter to summer?
c: It strengthens and moves toward the equator
questions.e: A weaker temperature contrast in summer gives a weaker jet at a higher latitude.

questions.q: Near which latitude is the subtropical jet found?
questions.e: The subtropical jet lies at the poleward edge of the Hadley cell, about 30 degrees.

questions.q: Where does FAA AC 00-6A place a preferred location for CAT relative to the jet stream?
c: On the cold (polar) side, in an upper trough
On the warm side, equatorward of the core
Only at the surface, below the jet core
Far from the jet, in the stratosphere
questions.e: FAA: wind speed falls off faster on the polar side, so shear is greater there.

sources: FAA Advisory Circular 00-6A, Aviation Weather: jet stream 50 kt minimum, dimensions, winter strength and southward shift, CAT on the cold side
LibreTexts, Jet streams: polar jet near 50 to 60 degrees and about 10 km; subtropical jet near 30 degrees and about 13 km; stronger in winter; cores often above 100 kt
Royal Meteorological Society, Jet streams: about 30,000 ft, average about 110 mph, polar jet strongest in winter, flight times
AMS Glossary, Jet stream: marked on upper-level charts at 50 kt or more (agrees with FAA AC 00-6A)

NWS Louisville, Jet streaks: upper divergence at the right entrance; MetEd jet streak circulation lab: divergence right entrance and left exit, convergence left entrance and right exit; EUMeTrain: cyclogenesis favoured at left exit and right entrance; University at Albany SHW Ch. 7: same quadrant pattern

Royal Meteorological Institute of Belgium (meteo.be), Courant-jet: minimum wind 30 m/s (108 km/h), no WMO attribution on the page; US Navy tpub Aerographer text: 50 kt, WMO dimensions (thousands of km long, hundreds wide, a few km deep)
unverified: Isotachs on 250 and 300 hPa charts: not checked.

The jet stream entrance and exit pattern now has four agreeing public sources (NWS Louisville, MetEd, EUMeTrain, Albany). Not checked in a Canadian publication. That the polar jet steers storms over Canada: standard teaching.

WMO 30 m/s (about 60 kt) threshold: the 30 m/s figure is corroborated by RMI Belgium but no page attributes it to the WMO. The WMO International Meteorological Vocabulary (WMO-No. 182) is a paid publication and was not available. The TC AIM jet stream wording was not found.

topics.title: Local winds (sea/land breeze, katabatic, valley)
lesson: Local winds develop when small-scale heating or terrain differences set up their own pressure gradients. They are strongest when the large-scale pressure gradient is weak.

list: Sea breeze: by day land heats faster than water, pressure falls over land, and air flows from sea to land (onshore). The sea breeze front brings a wind shift, a rapid drop in temperature and higher moisture, and clouds often form along it (NWS). Sea breezes are stronger than land breezes.
Land breeze: at night land cools faster, so air flows from land to sea (offshore). Weaker than the sea breeze.
Valley breeze: by day, sun heats slopes and air flows upslope and up-valley. The upslope flow on the heated slopes is called anabatic (AMS Glossary).
Mountain breeze: at night, valley walls cool and air flows downslope and down-valley. Cold air pooling in valleys can cause frost and fog.
Katabatic winds: cold air flowing down a slope under gravity. They are stronger than mountain breezes and can exceed 100 knots (NWS). Large-scale examples occur over ice sheets and glaciers.

Foehn or Chinook: warm, dry downslope wind on the lee of a mountain range (see adiabatic processes). The Chinook affects Alberta. NWS notes temperature can rise as much as 20 C in 1 hour with a sharp drop in relative humidity. Warming is mainly from compression, plus latent heat released if the air condensed on the windward side.

lesson.note: Local winds matter most when the large-scale pressure gradient is weak.

terms: Leading edge of the sea breeze, marked by a temperature drop and sometimes cloud lines.
Wind that flows upslope due to daytime heating.
Cold, dense air flowing downslope under gravity.
A foehn wind on the eastern slopes of the Rockies.

questions.q: When and in which direction does a sea breeze typically blow?
questions.e: Daytime land heating draws cooler air in from the sea.

questions.q: What is a katabatic wind?
c: Warm air flowing upslope in the afternoon
A wind blowing from the sea toward the land
A gust front produced by a thunderstorm
questions.e: Katabatic winds are gravity-driven drainage flows of cold air down slopes.

questions.q: Why does a land breeze occur at night?
c: Land cools faster than the sea, so pressure is higher over land
The sea cools faster than land at night, so pressure is higher over water
Coriolis deflection reverses sign after sunset and turns the wind offshore
Fronts usually move offshore at night and push the surface air out to sea
questions.e: A cooler, denser land surface creates higher pressure than over the warmer sea, driving offshore flow.

questions.q: A valley breeze generally blows:
c: Up the valley during the day
Down the valley during the day
questions.e: Daytime heating of slopes draws air upslope and up-valley.

questions.q: A Chinook is best described as:
c: A warm, dry downslope wind on the lee side of mountains
A cold, dense drainage wind flowing off glaciers and ice sheets
A moist onshore wind that brings fog to the windward coast
A tropical storm wind that crosses the Rockies in summer
questions.e: Chinooks are foehn-type winds: air warms by compression as it descends the lee slopes.

questions.q: What does the arrival of a sea breeze front at a coastal station usually bring?
c: A drop in temperature, a rise in humidity and a wind shift
A rise in temperature, a drop in humidity and no wind shift
No change in temperature, humidity or wind direction at all
Heavy snow and falling visibility with a strong easterly gale
questions.e: Cooler marine air replaces the warm land air.

questions.q: When are sea breezes strongest?
c: When the land-sea contrast is large and the gradient wind is weak
When it is cloudy and windy and the land is cooler than the sea
When a strong offshore gradient wind blows against the coast
When the land-sea temperature contrast is small and the sky is overcast
questions.e: Strong sunshine and a weak large-scale wind let the local circulation dominate.

questions.q: A mountain breeze at night blows:
c: Upslope and up-valley, as in the daytime
Always from the sea toward the land
Parallel to the coast, whatever the terrain
questions.e: Cooled slope air drains downhill at night.

questions.q: What does cold air pooling in valley bottoms on clear, calm nights produce?
c: Frost and fog in low areas
Strong winds on the valley floor
questions.e: Cold dense air collects in low ground and often reaches saturation.

questions.q: Which local wind is associated with the eastern slopes of the Rocky Mountains?
questions.e: The Chinook is the foehn wind of the Rockies.

questions.q: Compared with a sea breeze, a land breeze is generally:
c: Weaker, since the night-time temperature contrast is smaller
Stronger, since nights are colder and the contrast is much larger
About equal in strength, since both are driven by the same contrast
Possible only in winter, when the land is colder than the sea
questions.e: Land-sea contrasts are smaller at night, so land breezes are usually weaker.

questions.q: Per NWS training notes, how do katabatic winds compare with mountain breezes?
c: About the same strength as mountain breezes
Found only over open water, never on slopes
questions.e: NWS: katabatic winds are driven by cold air flowing down a slope, stronger than mountain breezes, and can exceed 100 knots.

Anabatic is now confirmed (AMS). Cold-air pooling giving frost and fog in valleys: standard teaching, not confirmed on any page read. Note the lesson labels the valley breeze 'anabatic'; AMS describes anabatic as upslope flow, so up-valley is a loose extension.
